claim: Life cover pays a benefit when the insured person dies, usually a lump sum and sometimes a monthly payment, in return for regular premiums. The benefit goes either to the beneficiaries named on the policy or into the estate, where debts are settled before heirs inherit under the will or the law of intestate succession. Some policies pay part of the benefit early on a terminal illness diagnosis.
title: What is life cover?
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). ASISA consumer education site. Generic definitions only; no product or insurer named in our copy.

claim: Fully underwritten cover asks detailed medical and family-history questions and may need tests such as blood tests; limited underwriting asks a few questions. Outcomes can be cover on standard terms, cover with exclusions, a higher premium or no cover. Limited-underwriting policies often exclude pre-existing conditions and can have a waiting period before natural-cause deaths are covered. A condition that is not disclosed can lead to a claim being rejected.
title: What does it mean if cover is fully or partially underwritten?
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). Used for the underwriting and disclosure lines on every cover type page.

claim: FSCA consumer booklet on life (long-term) insurance: the insurer pays a stated benefit, such as a lump sum, to the policyholder or nominated beneficiaries when an insured event such as death happens; underwriting decides whether cover is offered and on what terms; a consumer may take the policy away to read it, have it explained in plain language, and ask an adviser for proof of qualifications and for full details of fees and commission. It states a 31-day cooling-off period.
title: Learn more about Life Insurance (consumer booklet, 2021)
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). Booklet dated 2021, read 11 Oct 2026 (text extracted from the PDF). Consumer rights and the questions-to-ask lines.

claim: Disability cover pays either a lump sum or a monthly income (the income form is called income protection). The lump-sum form pays only for a permanent loss of the ability to work. Income benefits can run to a retirement age while the person cannot work. A policy may exclude work-related injuries or take Compensation Fund payments into account.
title: What is disability cover?
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). The page also says income benefits 'should' increase each year; our copy does not repeat that (rule S12).

claim: A disability claim succeeds only if the disability meets the policy's own definition: own occupation, own or similar occupation, or any occupation (own occupation is the widest and usually costs more), or a definition based on loss of function such as sight or a limb. In most cases a lump-sum claim needs the disability to be permanent; income products can also pay for temporary disability.
title: When will a disability policy pay out?
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). Definitions and permanence.

claim: FSCA consumer page: the two main kinds of disability cover are a capital (lump sum) benefit and an income benefit; the lump sum pays once the disability is shown to be permanent; the income benefit pays monthly for temporary or permanent disability and stops on recovery, death or the end of the policy.
title: Disability Cover
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). Template error at source: both headings read 'Income protector', the first section describes lump-sum cover. Used for the two kinds and when each stops.

claim: Severe illness cover, also called dread disease or critical illness cover, pays a lump sum on diagnosis of a serious illness listed in the policy, such as cancer or a heart attack. Unlike lump-sum disability cover it can pay even when recovery is expected, and the money can be used for costs other than medical bills. Some policies also cover serious injuries.
title: What is severe illness cover?
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). Definition.

claim: The original core conditions of severe illness cover are cancer, heart attack, stroke and coronary bypass surgery; policies now list from under a hundred to about three hundred conditions, with their own definitions and tiered payment levels, which makes them hard to compare. Many policies pay only if the person survives a set number of days (often 14 or 28) after diagnosis.
title: What illness does my severe illness policy cover?
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). Conditions lists, tiers, survival period.

claim: ASISA Standard on Disclosures for Critical Illness Products (updated 19 March 2025): standard definitions for heart attack, cancer, stroke and coronary bypass surgery at four severity levels (A most severe to D least); each insurer's quote and policy show what share of the benefit it pays at each level; a claimant declined under the insurer's own definition can ask for the claim to be assessed against the standard definitions. Binding on ASISA members.
title: Standard on Disclosures for Critical Illness Products
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). Read at source 11 Oct 2026. The percentages are set by each insurer; our copy quotes none.

claim: Income protection pays a monthly income instead of a lump sum, based on current income, and can run to a retirement age chosen in the policy (between 55 and 70 on the page). Temporary cover usually pays for 6, 12 or 24 months; permanent and partial disability cover are also offered.
title: What is an income protection policy?
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). Definition and benefit terms.

claim: On income protection the waiting period runs from the start of each claim, not only from the start of the policy, and applies to every claim; the policyholder chooses its length (employees often match it to sick leave); a longer waiting period means a lower premium; a relapse within a set period after returning to work usually does not restart it. Insurers also call this a deferment or deferred period.
title: Why are waiting periods important on income protection policies?
note: Read at source on 11 Oct 2026 (desk research). The 'deferment' synonym is insurer usage (1Life glossary, ASISA psychiatric-claims guideline 31 Mar 2026, seen in a search excerpt only); our copy says the policy wording decides which term it uses.

claim: Questions to ask about group life and disability cover, grounded in the Policyholder Protection Rules: is the disability benefit a lump sum or an income, when does the income stop, what is the waiting period, is temporary disability covered, which disability definition applies, what are the exclusions, is there a severe illness benefit.

claim: A death must be reported to the Master within 14 days. If the value of the estate exceeds R250 000, letters of executorship must be issued; for smaller estates letters of authority are issued under section 18(3) of the Administration of Estates Act. Documents include the death notice (J294), the death certificate, a next-of-kin affidavit (J192) where there is no will, an inventory (J243) and the executor's acceptance (J190); for smaller estates, an acceptance of the Master's directions (J155). Faxed documents are not accepted. Since 10 Oct 2023 estates can be registered online for the Johannesburg, Durban, Cape Town, Pretoria and Thohoyandou offices; original wills are still lodged in person.
title: Deceased Estates: How to report
publisher: Master of the High Court (Department of Justice and Constitutional Development)
note: Read at source on 18 Oct 2026 (docs/WILLS-ESTATE-SOURCES-2026-10-18.md).

claim: A person of 16 or older who is mentally capable can make a will. Witnesses must be 14 or older and competent to give evidence. A copy of a will is not deemed a valid will. If the testator cannot sign, a Commissioner of Oaths must certify the will. A beneficiary who signs as a witness, or that person's spouse, may lose the benefit. The executor's fee is 3.5% unless the will sets another fee. A bequest to a former spouse is treated as revoked if the testator dies within three months of the divorce. A will can be amended by a codicil, which must meet the same formalities.
title: Wills
publisher: Master of the High Court (Department of Justice and Constitutional Development)
note: Read at source on 18 Oct 2026 (docs/WILLS-ESTATE-SOURCES-2026-10-18.md).

claim: Without a valid will, the Intestate Succession Act sets the order of heirs: the spouse and descendants first, then parents, then brothers and sisters, then other blood relatives. With a spouse and descendants, the spouse inherits a child's share or R250 000, whichever is greater, and the rest is shared by the descendants. With more than one spouse, each spouse is entitled to at least R250 000 where the estate allows. In a marriage in community of property, the surviving spouse's half of the joint estate is not inherited under these rules. The estate goes to the state only if there are no relatives at all. Where there is a spouse and no descendants, the spouse inherits the estate; where there are descendants and no spouse, the descendants inherit it. Worked example on the page: an estate of R2 000 000 with one spouse and three children gives each of the four R500 000. If the estate cannot give each spouse R250 000, the spouses share it equally and the descendants receive nothing. The rules cover spouses in Muslim and Hindu marriages and adopted children.
title: Intestate Succession
publisher: Master of the High Court (Department of Justice and Constitutional Development)
note: Read at source on 18 Oct 2026 (docs/WILLS-ESTATE-SOURCES-2026-10-18.md).

claim: The Guardian's Fund holds money for minors, people unable to manage their own affairs, unborn heirs and missing heirs. Interest is compounded monthly and runs until five years after the money becomes claimable; unclaimed money is forfeited after 30 years. Maintenance such as school fees, clothing and medical costs can be paid from the interest, or from capital up to R250 000, on application (form J341). A child claims at 18, or at another age set in the will (form J251). The Master charges no administration fee. Unclaimed amounts are published every September. Claimants are verified, including with fingerprints. Tracing agents may not buy claims.
title: Guardians and Custodians (Guardian's Fund)
publisher: Master of the High Court (Department of Justice and Constitutional Development)
note: Read at source on 18 Oct 2026 (docs/WILLS-ESTATE-SOURCES-2026-10-18.md).

claim: If the value of an estate is R250 000 or less, a Master's representative is appointed, who usually does not lodge an account unless there are minor heirs. The executor lodges the liquidation and distribution account within six months of appointment and distributes the estate within two months after the account has lain open for inspection. The executor's fee is 3.5% of the gross assets plus 6% of income collected after death, with a minimum of R350.

Helpline 012 406 4805.

claim: The estate duty abatement is R3.5 million for deaths from 1 March 2007, and any portion a person did not use rolls over to the estate of the surviving spouse, up to R7 million in total. What is left to a surviving spouse is deductible under section 4(q) of the Estate Duty Act. A deceased estate is a separate taxpayer whose tax year starts the day after death.

claim: A surviving spouse can claim reasonable maintenance needs from the estate until death or remarriage, so far as the survivor cannot provide for them from their own means and earnings (section 2(1)). The claim ranks with a dependent child's maintenance claim, and both are reduced proportionately if the estate cannot cover them (section 2(3)(b)). The executor may settle the claim by agreement, including by creating a trust (section 2(3)(d)). Section 3 lists the factors: the size of the estate, the survivor's means and earning capacity, the standard of living during the marriage and the survivor's age.
title: Maintenance of Surviving Spouses Act 27 of 1990
note: Read at source on 18 Oct 2026 (docs/WILLS-ESTATE-SOURCES-2026-10-18.md).

claim: A parent who is the sole guardian of a child may appoint a person as guardian of the child in the event of the parent's death (section 27(1)(a)), and the appointment must be contained in a will made by the parent (section 27(2)).

note: Read at source on 18 Oct 2026 (docs/WILLS-ESTATE-SOURCES-2026-10-18.md).

claim: A will is valid if it is signed at the end by the testator in the presence of two or more competent witnesses who sign in the presence of the testator and of each other, and, where it has more than one page, each page other than the last is signed by the testator (section 2(1)(a)). A court can order the Master to accept a document that does not meet the formalities if it was intended as the will (section 2(3)). A person who signs as a witness, or writes the will, is disqualified from receiving a benefit under it, and being named as executor, trustee or guardian counts as a benefit (section 4A).
title: Wills Act 7 of 1953 (consolidated text)
note: Read at source on 18 Oct 2026 (docs/WILLS-ESTATE-SOURCES-2026-10-18.md).
